concepts.name: Magnetic poles
concepts.statement: All magnets attract iron, but a magnet brought near another magnet may attract it or repel it, because every magnet has two ends that behave differently. Suspend a magnet freely and one end points toward the north. The two ends are the north magnetic pole and the south magnetic pole, named for the directions they seek. Every later rule of the chapter, from the direction of a field line to the torque on a loop, uses these two poles.

concepts.name: Like poles repel
concepts.statement: Bring two magnets together and you find that two north poles push each other apart, two south poles do the same, and a north pole and a south pole pull together. Compare this with the electrostatic rule, unlike charges attract and like charges repel. The two look alike, and it is tempting to carry the whole of electrostatics across, but later sections show where the analogy holds and where it breaks.

concepts.name: No magnetic monopoles
concepts.statement: Cut a bar magnet in half and you do not get a north pole in one hand and a south pole in the other; you get two shorter magnets, each with both poles. Cut again and the same thing happens, down to the iron atom itself. This is where the analogy with charge fails, since a positive charge and a negative charge separate easily, and it is the fact that later forces the chapter to explain all magnetism as current: a current loop always produces a pair of poles and never a single one.

concepts.name: North magnetic pole
concepts.statement: The north magnetic pole of a magnet is the end or side that is attracted toward Earth's geographic north pole, the end that points north when the magnet is free to turn.

concepts.name: South magnetic pole
concepts.statement: The south magnetic pole of a magnet is the end or side that is attracted toward Earth's geographic south pole.

concepts.name: Ferromagnetic materials and magnetization
concepts.statement: Only a few materials, iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium and some rare earth alloys among them, show strong magnetic effects. These are called ferromagnetic, after ferrum, the Latin word for iron. They do more than respond to a magnet: they can be magnetized themselves, which means they can be induced to be magnetic or made into permanent magnets, and this is why a magnet held near an unmagnetized piece of iron attracts it.

concepts.name: Magnetic domains
concepts.statement: Inside a ferromagnetic material there are regions called domains, each of which acts like a small bar magnet because the poles of its individual atoms are aligned. In an unmagnetized object the domains are small and point in random directions, so their effects cancel. In an external magnetic field the domains that already point the right way grow at the expense of the others and the rest swing into line, and the material as a whole becomes a magnet. Heating it and cooling it, or tapping it while the field is applied, makes the alignment permanent.

concepts.name: Curie temperature
concepts.statement: Thermal motion works against the alignment of domains, so heating a permanent magnet in the absence of another magnet demagnetizes it, as do hard blows. For each ferromagnetic material there is a well-defined temperature, the Curie temperature, above which it cannot be magnetized at all; for iron it is 1043 K, which is 770 °C and well above room temperature. Some elements and alloys have Curie temperatures below room temperature and are ferromagnetic only when they are cold.

concepts.name: Electromagnet
concepts.statement: Oersted found in 1820 that a current-carrying wire deflects a compass needle, the first evidence that moving charge has anything to do with magnets. Using an electric current to make a magnet is called electromagnetism, and a magnet made this way is an electromagnet. Iron filings scattered around a current-carrying coil form the same pattern they form around a bar magnet. An electromagnet also has north and south poles that cannot be separated and that repel and attract by the same rule, so the two kinds of magnet are the same kind of thing.

concepts.name: Current as the source of magnetism
concepts.statement: An electromagnet makes a field with a current, and a ferromagnet does too, at a scale too small to see. An electron in orbit about a nucleus is a closed current loop, the electron's spin is a second current, and both produce a magnetic field with a north pole and a south pole. Ferromagnetism is the cooperative alignment of these spins. Isolated poles are never found, because a current loop always produces a pair of poles. The rest of the chapter rests on this idea.

concepts.name: Electromagnetism
concepts.statement: Electromagnetism is the use of electric currents to produce magnetism, and more broadly the single subject that electricity and magnetism become once a current is known to make a magnetic field.

concepts.name: Magnetized
concepts.statement: A material is magnetized when it has been turned into a magnet, either induced to be magnetic for a time or made into a permanent magnet.

concepts.name: Magnetic field
concepts.statement: The magnetic field, traditionally called the B-field, is the representation of magnetic forces. Like the gravitational and electric fields, it maps the forces that surround an object and can act on another object at a distance, and it represents the object that generates it, not the probe that tests it.

concepts.name: Direction of magnetic field lines
concepts.statement: We draw the field with magnetic field lines, a pictorial tool for showing its strength and its direction. The direction of the lines is the direction in which the north end of a small compass needle points, so you can check it with a compass on a table. Small compasses do not disturb the field they test, just as a small test charge does not disturb an electric field, so the map they trace is a map of the magnet alone.

concepts.name: Rules for magnetic field lines
concepts.statement: Mapping many fields has settled four rules. The field is tangent to the field line at every point, so a compass lies along the line. The strength of the field is proportional to how closely the lines are packed, exactly to the number of lines crossing a unit area held perpendicular to them. Lines never cross, because the field has one value at each point in space. And the lines are continuous closed loops with no beginning and no end, which is the deepest of the four, since electric field lines begin and end on charges and magnetic lines have no monopoles to begin or end on.

concepts.name: Magnetic field lines
concepts.statement: Magnetic field lines are a pictorial representation of a magnetic field: the field points along them, and they are closer together where the field is stronger.

concepts.name: Magnetic force on a moving charge
concepts.statement: A magnetic field exerts a force on a charge only while the charge moves. The size of that force is the charge times the speed times the field strength times the sine of the angle between the velocity and the field. The sine matters as much as the rest: a charge moving along a field line feels no force at all, and a charge moving across the lines feels the most. This force is often called the Lorentz force, and it is how one magnet pushes another, since every magnet is made of moving charge.

concepts.name: Magnetic field strength
concepts.statement: Field lines show what a magnetic field looks like; turning the force law around says what its strength is. Solving for $B$ defines the strength of a field as the force per unit charge per unit velocity, measured across the field, just as the electric field strength is the force per unit charge. So we know the field only through what it does to a moving charge.

concepts.name: Tesla
concepts.statement: Because the sine is a pure number, the unit of magnetic field strength follows from the definition: one tesla is one newton per coulomb per metre per second, which is one newton per ampere-metre. A smaller unit, the gauss, is $10^{-4}$ tesla. The strongest permanent magnets reach about 2 T, and superconducting electromagnets 10 T or more. The Earth's field at the surface is only about $5 \times 10^{-5}$ T, half a gauss, which is why you never feel the Earth pushing on the charge in your pocket.

concepts.name: Right hand rule 1
concepts.statement: The direction of the magnetic force is perpendicular to the plane formed by the velocity and the field, which is not a direction that can be read off a flat drawing without a convention, so the book gives one. Point the thumb of the right hand along the velocity, the fingers along the field, and the force on a positive charge comes out of the palm. One velocity, one thumb; many field lines, many fingers; the force is the way you would push. The force on a negative charge is exactly opposite.

concepts.name: Force and the sign of charge
concepts.statement: Right hand rule 1 applies to a positive charge, and the force on a negative charge moving the same way points in exactly the opposite direction. The charges that actually move in a wire are electrons, so throughout the chapter you will translate between the direction of a conventional current and the direction the carriers travel. The reversal also lets the Hall effect reveal which sign of carrier is moving.

concepts.name: Gauss
concepts.statement: The gauss is a smaller unit of magnetic field strength than the tesla, with $1\;\text{G} = 10^{-4}\;\text{T}$.

concepts.name: Magnetic force doing no work
concepts.statement: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, and a force perpendicular to the motion does no work. So the kinetic energy of the particle and its speed do not change: only the direction of the motion is affected. This is the single fact that decides everything else in the section, because a force of constant magnitude that is always perpendicular to the velocity is what uniform circular motion requires.

concepts.name: Circular motion in a magnetic field
concepts.statement: When a charge moves perpendicular to a uniform field, the magnetic force is the centripetal force, so $qvB$ equals $mv^2/r$. You have already solved circular motion in Chapter 6; here you need only recognise which force plays the centripetal part. In a vacuum the magnetic field alone decides the motion, and the particle circles forever at constant speed.

concepts.name: Radius of a charged particle’s path
concepts.statement: Solving the centripetal equation for the radius gives the mass times the speed divided by the charge times the field. Everything the chapter does with curved tracks follows from this fraction: a heavier or faster particle swings wider, and a stronger field or a larger charge pulls the circle tighter. Fixing the speed, the charge and the field makes the radius proportional to the mass, which is how a mass spectrometer weighs an ion. It is also why a magnet held against the glass turns an electron in a television tube through a circle less than a millimetre across.

concepts.name: Spiral along field lines
concepts.statement: Only the component of the velocity perpendicular to the field bends; the component along the field stays the same, since the magnetic force is zero for motion parallel to the lines. A particle that enters at an angle therefore circles about a field line while drifting along it, in a spiral rather than a circle. Charged particles approaching a magnetic field are far more likely to spiral about the lines than to cross them. That explains the aurora, the shape of the tracks in Figure 22.20 and the whole of the next idea.

concepts.name: Magnetic mirror
concepts.statement: Where the field lines crowd together, the field grows stronger along the direction of travel. The force then has a component that slows the particle's motion along the line and can turn it back. A region of strong field at each end therefore traps a particle bouncing between them, which is a magnetic mirror. The Earth is such a trap. Its two Van Allen belts hold particles from the Sun and from deep space, which migrate along the field lines and reflect away from the poles. Those that do enter the atmosphere near the poles light the aurora and give a higher radiation dose there than at the equator.

concepts.name: Confining and steering charged particles
concepts.statement: Engineers build the same trapping on purpose. Accelerators use magnetic fields not only to bend a beam around its ring but to focus it and hold it together against the repulsion of its own like charges. A tokamak bends a solenoid into a doughnut so that the charged particles of a plasma circle the field lines without ever reaching the wall, the leading hope for containing a fusion reaction. A microwave oven's magnetron holds oscillating electrons the same way. All of these apply one idea.

concepts.name: Hall effect
concepts.statement: A magnetic field acts on the charges moving inside a conductor just as it acts on a free charge, and since the charges cannot leave the metal, they pile up on one side and leave the other side with the opposite sign. The separated charge makes an electric field across the conductor, and that field pushes the carriers back. The pile-up therefore stops almost at once, at the point where the electric force $qE$ equals the magnetic force $qvB$, so that $E = vB$. The voltage this separation produces across the conductor is the Hall emf.

concepts.name: Hall emf
concepts.statement: For a uniform field across a uniform conductor the electric field is uniform too, so the voltage is the field times the width, $E = \varepsilon/l$. Putting that into the balance gives the Hall emf as the field times the width times the speed, when the three are mutually perpendicular. It is a small voltage, tens of microvolts for blood in an artery, and the section is careful to say so, since the difficulty of measuring it against the millivolts of a heartbeat is why a Hall flow probe applies an alternating field.

concepts.name: Finding the sign of charge carriers
concepts.statement: Reverse the sign of the carriers and, for the same conventional current, they move the other way. The magnetic force pushes them to the same side, but they carry the opposite charge there, so the Hall emf changes sign. Knowing the directions of the field and the current therefore tells you the sign of whatever carries the current. Historically, this showed that electrons carry the current in metals and that positive carriers do so in some semiconductors.

concepts.name: Hall probes and flow meters
concepts.statement: Two applications follow directly from the formula. Run a known current through a small conductor and the Hall emf measures the field, which is a Hall probe; they can be made very small and, once calibrated, very accurate. Or fix the field and the width and the Hall emf measures the speed of whatever is moving, which is how blood flow in an artery and water flow in a pipe are measured without touching the fluid. Here the sign of the emf depends only on the directions of the field and the velocity, not on the sign of the charges, so a fluid carrying both signs still gives a reading.

concepts.name: Force on a current-carrying wire
concepts.statement: Charges cannot escape a wire, so the magnetic force on the charges moving inside it passes to the wire itself. Add the force on every carrier in a length of wire, and recognise that the number of carriers per unit volume times the charge times the drift velocity times the area is the current. The force on one charge then becomes a force on the wire: the current times the length in the field times the field times the sine of the angle between the current and the field. This derivation bridges a law about particles and a law about circuits.

concepts.name: Force per unit length on a wire
concepts.statement: Dividing by the length gives the force per metre of wire. Use this form whenever the wire is long or its length is not given, as for a lightning bolt, a power line or the two parallel conductors of 22.10. It is the same result written so that only the current, the field and the angle appear.

concepts.name: Right hand rule 1 for a current
concepts.statement: The same right hand rule gives the direction of the force on a wire as on a single charge, with the thumb now along the current rather than along one charge's velocity. The substitution is exact because a conventional current points the way positive carriers would move, so you need no second rule.

concepts.name: Magnetohydrodynamic pump
concepts.statement: If the current runs through a conducting fluid rather than a wire, the force falls on the fluid and pushes it along the tube, and the pump has no moving parts at all. That is attractive for a hot or chemically active liquid such as the sodium in some nuclear reactors, for an experimental artificial heart, and for a submarine drive that would run more quietly than a propeller. The direction of the force does not depend on the sign of the carriers, so a fluid carrying both signs still moves one way.

concepts.name: Torque on a current loop
concepts.statement: Put a rectangular loop of wire on a shaft in a uniform field. The forces on its two vertical sides are equal and opposite, so the loop does not move off, but each produces a torque about the shaft in the same sense, so the loop turns. Adding the two torques gives the width times the force. Putting $F = IlB$ into it and recognising the width times the height as the area gives the torque as the number of turns times the current times the area times the field times the sine of the angle. The derivation uses a rectangle, but the result holds for a loop of any shape.

concepts.name: Torque and angle
concepts.statement: The angle in the formula is between the field and the perpendicular to the loop, so the torque is greatest when the loop's plane lies along the field and falls to zero when the loop faces the field squarely. Past that point the sine changes sign and so does the torque, which means that a loop left to itself does not keep turning: it oscillates back and forth about the position of zero torque, exactly as a compass needle settles onto a field line.

concepts.name: Net force on a loop
concepts.statement: The forces on the top and bottom segments of the loop are vertical, parallel to the shaft, equal in size and opposite in direction, so they neither turn the loop nor push it anywhere. The forces on the two vertical sides are equal and opposite as well. The loop therefore feels no net force in a uniform field, only a torque, and a motor turns without wandering across the room.

concepts.name: Brushes keep a motor turning
concepts.statement: A coil that only oscillates is no use, so a motor reverses the current each time the coil passes the position of zero torque, using automatic switches called brushes. The torque then always acts the same way round and the coil keeps turning in one direction, which is how electrical energy is turned into mechanical work. This is the whole of the motor: a loop, a field, and a switch that changes the current twice a revolution.

concepts.name: Analog meter as a motor
concepts.statement: An analog meter is built the same way, but its magnet poles are shaped so that the field stays perpendicular to the loop over a wide range of angles. The sine is then always about one, the torque depends on the current and not on the angle, and a spring supplies a counter-torque that grows with the deflection, so the needle's position is proportional to the current. A sensitive galvanometer for a voltmeter or an ammeter wants a large loop area, a strong field and low-resistance coils.

concepts.name: Number of turns
concepts.statement: A coil is a wire wound into loops, and its number of turns $N$ is how many loops it has. Each turn feels the same torque in a field and encloses the same flux, so many quantities of a coil are $N$ times those of a single loop.

concepts.name: Electric motor
concepts.statement: An electric motor is a loop of wire, or a coil of many loops, mounted on a shaft in a magnetic field, so that the torque the field exerts on its current turns the shaft.

concepts.name: Field of a long straight wire
terms: magnetic field strength (magnitude) produced by a long straight current-carrying wire
concepts.statement: Experiment gives the field round a long straight wire as the permeability of free space times the current, divided by two pi times the shortest distance to the wire. The field falls off as one over the distance, not one over the distance squared, and, because the wire is long, it does not depend on where along the wire the point is. The section's own example is the most useful reading of it: 25 A in a wire makes twice the Earth's field 5.0 cm away, which is why an overhead power line disturbs a surveyor's compass.

concepts.name: Right hand rule 2
concepts.statement: Compasses set around a straight wire show that the field lines are circles centred on the wire, and the second right hand rule gives the sense of the circles: point the thumb along the current and the fingers curl the way the field goes. It holds for any segment of current, not only a straight wire, so the same rule gives the field of a loop and of a solenoid. The first right hand rule gives a force and this one gives a field, and keeping the two apart is most of the work.

concepts.name: Permeability of free space
concepts.statement: The constant in the field formulas, $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A, is the permeability of free space, one of the basic constants of nature and the magnetic counterpart of the permittivity that appeared in the electric field. Its value is exact rather than measured, which is what makes the definition of the ampere in 22.10 possible, and the book notes that it is related to the speed of light, a connection the later chapters make good.

concepts.name: Ampere’s law
concepts.statement: Every segment of a current makes a field like a short piece of a long straight wire, and the field of a current of any shape is the vector sum of the fields of its segments. Stating that for one segment is the Biot-Savart law, and summing it with calculus gives Ampere's law, which relates field and current in general. Ampere's law is one of Maxwell's equations, the four that describe all electromagnetic phenomena; the book keeps the general features, the right hand rule and the rules for field lines, and leaves the integrals to a later course.

concepts.name: Field at the center of a loop
terms: magnetic field strength at the center of a circular loop
concepts.statement: The field of a current loop is complicated everywhere except at its centre, and there it is simple: the permeability times the current divided by twice the radius, and $N$ times that for a flat coil of $N$ loops. The larger the loop, the weaker its centre field, because the current is farther away. Outside the loop the field has the shape of a bar magnet's, which puts numbers to the iron-filing pattern of 22.2.

concepts.name: Field inside a solenoid
terms: magnetic field strength inside a solenoid
concepts.statement: Wind the wire into a long coil and the fields of the turns add inside and very nearly cancel outside. The field inside is uniform in magnitude and direction over most of the coil's length, and the field just outside is nearly zero. Its strength is the permeability times the number of turns per unit length times the current, with no radius in it at all. That is why a solenoid, as in an MRI magnet, is the way to make a strong and uniform field over a large volume.

concepts.name: Solenoid
concepts.statement: A solenoid is a thin wire wound into a long coil, and the number of loops per unit length, $n = N/l$, describes how tightly it is wound.

concepts.name: Biot-Savart law
concepts.statement: The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field made by each small segment of a current, so that the field of any current is the sum of the fields of its segments.

concepts.name: Force between parallel currents
concepts.statement: Nothing new is needed for this result, only the two things the chapter already has: the first wire makes a field at the second, and the second wire feels a force in that field. Putting the straight-wire field into the force on a current and dividing by the length gives the force per unit length as the permeability times the two currents divided by two pi times the separation. By Newton's third law each wire feels the same size of force, which is why one number serves for both.

concepts.name: Attraction and repulsion of currents
concepts.statement: Following the two right hand rules around gives the sense of the force: wires carrying current the same way pull together, and wires carrying current opposite ways push apart. This is the reverse of what you might guess from like charges repelling, so check it once with your hand. The hot and neutral wires of an appliance cord and the two conductors of a light-rail line are everyday cases of it.

concepts.name: Pinch effect
concepts.statement: Because parallel currents attract, a current spread over a region squeezes itself into a narrower one. In an electric arc or a plasma this is the pinch effect, and it is not a curiosity: in a large circuit breaker it concentrates the arc between the plates that are trying to interrupt the current, burning holes and sometimes igniting the equipment. The jets of ionized material in a solar flare are shaped the same way.

concepts.name: Definition of the ampere
concepts.statement: Putting one ampere in each of two wires one metre apart makes a force of exactly $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N/m, exactly because the permeability of free space is itself defined as exactly $4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A. That statement, run backwards, is the operational definition of the ampere, and with it the coulomb, since one coulomb is the charge that flows in one second at one ampere. In practice a current balance uses coils a few centimetres apart rather than infinite wires, and measuring force is the most accurate way known of fixing both units.

concepts.name: Mass spectrometer
concepts.statement: The radius of a charged particle's circle is its mass times its speed divided by its charge times the field, so if the speed, the charge and the field are all fixed, the radius is simply proportional to the mass. That is a mass spectrometer: an ion source, a stage that fixes the speed, and a uniform field in which each ion swings round an arc whose width reports its mass. The charge comes in multiples of the electron's, so it is easy to allow for. The instrument identifies chemicals and biological molecules by their mass-to-charge ratios and measures the isotope tracers used in medicine.

concepts.name: Velocity selector
concepts.statement: Cross an electric field with a magnetic field so that they push a moving charge opposite ways, and only the particles for which the two forces balance go straight through. Setting $qE$ equal to $qvB$ cancels the charge and leaves the speed as the electric field divided by the magnetic field, which means the selected speed does not depend on the charge or the mass of the particle at all and can be dialled by changing either field. It is the stage that makes a mass spectrometer's arcs mean something.

concepts.name: Steering an electron beam
concepts.statement: A cathode ray tube, an old computer monitor, an x-ray machine and a two-mile linear accelerator are all versions of the same electron gun, and many of them use magnetic fields to point the beam. Two pairs of coils, one for the vertical and one for the horizontal, bend the electrons to wherever they are wanted on the screen. The rays are called cathode rays because they start at the cathode in the gun.

concepts.name: Magnetic resonance imaging
concepts.statement: Certain nuclei, hydrogen's single proton above all, have small magnetic fields of their own, like the current loops of this chapter. Put them in a strong external field and they are pushed into one of two energy states, and a radio signal of exactly the right frequency flips them between the two. The frequency that is absorbed and re-emitted depends on the nucleus, on its chemical surroundings and on the field strength, so sweeping the field across the body makes position report itself as frequency, and the strength of the returned signal reports how much of that nucleus is there. That is nuclear magnetic resonance, and imaging with it is MRI.

concepts.name: Biomagnetic measurement
concepts.statement: Currents in nerve cells and in the heart make magnetic fields like any other currents, and those fields can be recorded without touching the body: the heart's is a magnetocardiogram and the brain's a magnetoencephalogram. They are between a million and a hundred million times weaker than the Earth's field, so they are read with a SQUID, a superconducting detector that works at liquid helium temperatures. They report activity rather than structure, which is what makes them useful for epilepsy and for fetal studies and different from an electrocardiogram.

concepts.name: Nuclear magnetic resonance
concepts.statement: Nuclear magnetic resonance is the interaction of an applied magnetic field with the nuclei of certain atoms, whose own small magnetic fields line up with it and absorb radio waves at a frequency set by the field strength.

concepts.name: Magnetocardiogram
concepts.statement: A magnetocardiogram is a recording of the heart's magnetic field as it beats.

concepts.name: Magnetoencephalogram
concepts.statement: A magnetoencephalogram is a measurement of the brain's magnetic field.
